topics.name: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios of a Line in Space
topics.summary: The direction of a line in space is described by direction cosines \( (l,m,n) \) (satisfying \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \)) or, more conveniently, by any proportional triple of direction ratios \( (a,b,c) \). Direction ratios of the line joining two points are just the coordinate differences — no normalisation is ever required to use them.
key_formulas: Direction cosines from direction ratios: \( l=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}} \), and similarly for \(m,n\)
Direction ratios of the line joining \( (x_1,y_1,z_1) \) and \( (x_2,y_2,z_2) \): \( (x_2-x_1,\ y_2-y_1,\ z_2-z_1) \)

worked_example.problem: Find the direction cosines of the line with direction ratios \( (2,\ -3,\ 6) \).

common_mistakes: Using the cartesian symmetric-form denominators as the direction ratios directly, but then needlessly (and often incorrectly) trying to normalise them into direction cosines first

Confusing the direction-ratio subtraction order, or reading off a coefficient without adjusting for a multiplier in front of a variable (e.g. treating \( \dfrac{2x-4}{3} \) as if the direction ratio were simply \(3\), instead of rewriting it as \( \dfrac{x-2}{3/2} \) first)
Using \( l+m+n=1 \) instead of the correct identity \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \)

topics.name: Equation of a Line in Space: Vector and Cartesian Forms, Angle Between Two Lines
topics.summary: A line in space is fixed by a point and a direction, written in vector form \( \vec r=\vec a+\lambda\vec b \) or cartesian symmetric form \( \dfrac{x-x_1}{a}=\dfrac{y-y_1}{b}=\dfrac{z-z_1}{c} \). The angle between two lines compares their direction VECTORS with a cosine formula — easy to confuse with the (sine-based) line–plane angle formula from a later topic.
key_formulas: Angle between two lines: \( \cos\theta=\dfrac{|\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2|}{|\vec b_1||\vec b_2|} \)
Parallel lines: direction ratios proportional. Perpendicular lines: \( a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0 \)

worked_example.problem: Find the angle between the lines with direction ratios \( (2,\ 2,\ 1) \) and \( (4,\ 1,\ 8) \).
worked_example.solution:
\( \cos\theta=\dfrac{|2(4)+2(1)+1(8)|}{\sqrt{4+4+1}\cdot\sqrt{16+1+64}}=\dfrac{18}{3\cdot9}=\dfrac{2}{3} \).

This does not correspond to one of the standard angles in every textbook problem, but when it's engineered to (as in this chapter's question bank), \( \theta \) comes out to \(0^\circ\), \(30^\circ\), \(45^\circ\), \(60^\circ\) or \(90^\circ\).

common_mistakes: Using the sine formula \( \sin\theta=\dfrac{|\vec b\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec b||\vec n|} \) (meant for a line and a plane) instead of the cosine formula for two lines
Dropping the absolute value, so a negative dot product gives the obtuse supplementary angle instead of the acute angle between the lines
Using the two points' position vectors (instead of the direction vector) when writing or reading a vector-form equation

topics.name: Shortest Distance Between Two Lines (Skew and Parallel Lines)
topics.summary: Two lines in space are either intersecting, parallel, or skew. For skew lines, the shortest distance uses the cross product \( \vec b_1\times\vec b_2 \); for parallel lines that formula breaks down (since \( \vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\vec 0 \)) and a different formula is needed instead.
key_formulas: Skew lines: \( d=\left|\dfrac{(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\right| \)
Parallel lines (same \( \vec b \)): \( d=\dfrac{|\vec b\times(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)|}{|\vec b|} \)
Lines are skew when the scalar triple product \( (\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)\neq 0 \) and the direction ratios are not proportional

worked_example.problem: Find the shortest distance between the lines \( \vec r=\hat i+\lambda(2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k) \) and \( \vec r=(2\hat i-\hat j)+\mu(3\hat i-5\hat j+2\hat k) \).
worked_example.solution:
\( \vec b_1\times\vec b_2=(3,\ -1,\ -7) \), so \( |\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|=\sqrt{59} \).

\( (\vec a_2-\vec a_1)=(1,\ -1,\ 0) \), and the scalar triple product gives the numerator; dividing by \( \sqrt{59} \) gives the shortest distance.

common_mistakes: Applying the skew-line cross-product formula to parallel lines (where \( \vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\vec 0 \), so the formula is undefined) instead of switching to the parallel-line formula
Dropping the absolute value, producing a negative ‘distance’
Forgetting to take the square root of \( |\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|^2 \) in the denominator

topics.name: Equation of a Plane: Normal Form, Three-Point Form, and Angle Between Planes or a Line and a Plane
topics.summary: A plane can be described by its normal and one point on it (\( Ax+By+Cz=D \)), or by three non-collinear points on it (normal \( =\vec{PQ}\times\vec{PR} \)). Three related-but-different angle formulas apply depending on whether you're comparing two lines, two planes, or a line and a plane — the line–plane case uniquely uses sine, not cosine.
key_formulas: General form: \( Ax+By+Cz=D \), with \( (A,B,C) \) a normal vector
Three-point form: normal \( \vec n=\vec{PQ}\times\vec{PR} \); \( D=\vec n\cdot\vec{OP} \)
Angle between two planes: \( \cos\theta=\dfrac{|\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2|}{|\vec n_1||\vec n_2|} \)
Angle between a line and a plane: \( \sin\phi=\dfrac{|\vec b\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec b||\vec n|} \)

worked_example.problem: Find the equation of the plane through \( (1,\ 1,\ 1) \) with normal direction ratios \( (2,\ -1,\ 3) \).

common_mistakes: Using \( \sin\theta=\dfrac{|\vec b\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec b||\vec n|} \) (line–plane) in place of \( \cos\theta=\dfrac{|\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2|}{|\vec n_1||\vec n_2|} \) (plane–plane), or vice versa
Reading coefficients off a plane's equation before it has been fully rearranged into \( Ax+By+Cz=D \) form, missing a sign flip on a term moved across the equals sign
Using only one edge vector of a three-point plane as if it were the normal, instead of the cross product of two edge vectors

topics.name: Distance of a Point from a Plane, and Coplanarity of Two Lines
topics.summary: The distance of a point from a plane requires the plane's equation to be in the fully rearranged standard form first, and always carries an absolute value. Two lines are coplanar exactly when the scalar triple product of the connecting vector and the two direction vectors vanishes — the same test whether the direction vectors are given as ratios or as (unit-length) direction cosines.
key_formulas: Coplanarity of two lines: \( (\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)=0 \)

worked_example.problem: Find the distance of the point \( (2,\ 5,\ -3) \) from the plane \( 6x-3y+2z=4 \).

common_mistakes: Dropping the absolute value, giving a signed (sometimes negative) ‘distance’
Reading off \( a,b,c,d \) from a plane's equation that has not first been rearranged into standard \( ax+by+cz+d=0 \) form, missing a sign flip on a moved term
Assuming the coplanarity test only works with direction ratios and not with direction cosines (a unit-length scaling doesn't change the test's outcome)

questions.topic: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios of a Line in Space
questions.question: Points \( A(4,\ -2,\ 3) \) and \( B(0,\ 2,\ -5) \) are given. Find the direction ratios of line \( AB \), directed from \(A\) to \(B\).
questions.explanation:
Direction ratios of the line joining two points are simply the coordinate differences \( (x_2-x_1,\ y_2-y_1,\ z_2-z_1) \), taken directly \u2014 no normalisation is needed.

\( AB=(0-4,\ 2-(-2),\ -5-3)=(-4,\ 4,\ -8) \)
questions.hint: Subtract the coordinates of A from B, component by component — no need to divide by anything.
distractor_logic: Wrong: flipping the sign of only one component changes the direction (it is no longer proportional to the correct triple).
Wrong: this adds the coordinates instead of subtracting them.
Wrong: this swaps the x- and y-differences, which points along a different line.
Correct: direction ratios of the line through A and B are the coordinate differences (x2−x1, y2−y1, z2−z1).

questions.topic: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios of a Line in Space
questions.question: A line has direction ratios \( (0,\ -3,\ -4) \). Find its direction cosines.
questions.explanation:
Magnitude: \( \sqrt{0^2+(-3)^2+(-4)^2}=\sqrt{25}=5 \).

Direction cosines \( =\left(\dfrac{a}{k},\dfrac{b}{k},\dfrac{c}{k}\right) \), where \(k\) is this magnitude \u2014 giving \( \left(\dfrac{0}{5},\ \dfrac{-3}{5},\ \dfrac{-4}{5}\right) \).
questions.hint: Divide each direction ratio by \( \sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2} \); do not leave them un-normalised.
distractor_logic: Wrong: divides by \( |a|+|b|+|c|=7 \) instead of the magnitude \( \sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2} \).
Wrong: the sign of the middle component has been flipped, giving a different direction.
Wrong: these are the raw direction ratios, not divided by anything — they don't satisfy \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \).
Correct: direction cosines are the direction ratios each divided by the magnitude \( \sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}=5 \).

questions.topic: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios of a Line in Space
questions.question: A line makes angles with the coordinate axes such that \( \cos\alpha=\dfrac{-6}{7} \) and \( \cos\beta=\dfrac{2}{7} \). Using \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \), find \( \cos\gamma \) (taking the value that matches a line with direction ratios \( (-6,2,-3) \)).
questions.explanation:
\( n^2=1-l^2-m^2=1-\left(\dfrac{-6}{7}\right)^2-\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^2=\dfrac{9}{49} \).

So \( n=\dfrac{-3}{7} \) (matching the sign of the third direction ratio).
questions.hint: Use \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \) — it's a sum of squares, not a linear sum.
distractor_logic: Wrong: forgets to take the square root after computing \( 1-l^2-m^2 \).
Wrong: this is the correct magnitude but with the wrong sign.
Correct: from \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \), \( n=\pm\sqrt{1-l^2-m^2} \); taking the value consistent with the line gives \( n=\dfrac{-3}{7} \).
Wrong: incorrectly uses \( l+m+n=1 \) (a linear relation) instead of the actual identity \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \).

questions.topic: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios of a Line in Space
questions.question: Find the direction ratios of the line whose Cartesian equation is \( \dfrac{2x-4}{1}=\dfrac{y-2}{2}=\dfrac{z+1}{-2} \).
questions.explanation:
The \(x\)-term carries a coefficient, so rewrite \( 2x-4 \) as \( 2(x-(2)) \) first \u2014 the effective \(x\)-denominator becomes \( \dfrac{1}{2} \), not \(1\) as it first appears.

Clearing all denominators to compare with \( \dfrac{x-x_1}{a}=\dfrac{y-y_1}{b}=\dfrac{z-z_1}{c} \) gives direction ratios \( (1,\ 4,\ -4) \).
questions.hint: Before reading off the denominators, rewrite any term that has a coefficient on the variable in the form (variable − constant).
distractor_logic: Wrong: flips the sign of the first component.
Correct: rewrite the \(x\)-term as \( \dfrac{x-x_1}{a/2} \) first, then clear the fraction \u2014 the true direction ratios are \( (a,\ 2 b,\ 2 c) \).
Wrong: reads the denominators straight off without accounting for the \(2\) multiplying \(x\).
Wrong: swaps the first two components.

questions.topic: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios of a Line in Space
questions.question: A line has direction ratios \( (-1,\ 5,\ -1) \). Another line has direction ratios \( (0,\ -1,\ z) \) and is perpendicular to the first. Find \( z \).
questions.explanation:
Perpendicularity condition: \( a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0 \).

\( -1(0)+5(-1)+-1(z)=0\ \Rightarrow\ z=-5 \).
questions.hint: Perpendicular lines satisfy \( a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0 \), not a proportion.
distractor_logic: Wrong: sign of the correct value has been flipped.
Wrong: uses the parallel condition \( \dfrac{a_1}{a_2}=\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}=\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} \) instead of the perpendicularity condition.
Correct: perpendicularity needs \( a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0 \); solving for the unknown component gives this value.
Wrong: an arithmetic slip of one unit while solving the equation.

questions.question: A line has direction ratios in the proportion \( a:b:c=1:2:2 \). Find its direction cosines.
questions.explanation:
Take \( (a,b,c)=(1,2,2) \) (any scalar multiple works). Magnitude \( =\sqrt{1^2+2^2+2^2}=3 \).

Direction cosines \( =\left(\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \).

distractor_logic: Wrong: these are the direction ratios themselves, not normalised into direction cosines.
Wrong: two of the three signs have been flipped, giving a different direction.
Correct: direction ratios proportional to \( 1:2:2 \) give direction cosines \( \left(\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \) after dividing by \( \sqrt{1^2+2^2+2^2}=3 \).
Wrong: divides by \( |a|+|b|+|c| \) instead of the magnitude \( \sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2} \).

questions.topic: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios of a Line in Space
questions.question: A line makes equal angles with all three coordinate axes. Find its direction cosines (taking the positive octant direction).
questions.explanation:
Equal inclination \( \Rightarrow l=m=n \). Since \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \), \( 3l^2=1\Rightarrow l=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \).

So the direction cosines are \( \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right) \).
questions.hint: Set \( l=m=n \) and substitute into \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \).
distractor_logic: Correct: equal inclination gives \( l=m=n \); with \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \) this forces \( l=m=n=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \).
Wrong: the line is not equally inclined if one direction cosine has the opposite sign.
Wrong: these are direction ratios, not direction cosines (magnitude here is \( \sqrt3\), not \(1\)).
Wrong: uses \( l+m+n=1 \) instead of \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \).

questions.topic: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios of a Line in Space
questions.question: Find the direction ratios of a line that is perpendicular to both lines with direction ratios \( (-1,-1,2) \) and \( (-1,3,1) \).
questions.explanation:
A line perpendicular to two given directions has direction ratios given by their cross product.

\( (-1,-1,2)\times(-1,3,1)=(-7,\ -1,\ -4) \)
questions.hint: Use the cross product of the two given direction-ratio triples.
distractor_logic: Wrong: sign of the first component is flipped.
Wrong: swaps the first two components of the cross product.
Correct: a line perpendicular to two given lines has direction ratios along their cross product \( \vec{b_1}\times\vec{b_2} \).
Wrong: simply adds the two direction ratio triples — this does not give a line perpendicular to both.

questions.topic: Shortest Distance Between Two Lines (Skew and Parallel Lines)

questions.question: Line \( L_1 \) has direction cosines \( \left(\dfrac{1}{3},\ \dfrac{-2}{3},\ \dfrac{2}{3}\right) \) and passes through \( (-2,\ 0,\ -1) \). Line \( L_2 \) passes through \( (1,\ 1,\ -1) \) with direction ratios \( (1,\ -3,\ 2) \). Are the lines coplanar?
options: Coplanar only when direction cosines are used instead of direction ratios
Cannot be tested using direction cosines, only direction ratios
questions.explanation:
Direction cosines are just direction ratios \( (1,\ -2,\ 2) \) scaled to unit length (T1 skill) \u2014 scaling doesn't change direction.

Scalar triple product \( (\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)=6 \) (T5 skill), so the lines are not coplanar (skew).
questions.hint: Direction cosines are just a scaled version of direction ratios — use them directly in the scalar triple product test.
distractor_logic: Wrong: Direction cosines are just a particular (unit-length) scaling of direction ratios — the coplanarity test works identically with either, since scaling a direction vector doesn't change the direction it represents.
Wrong: This needs the scalar triple product to be exactly zero — check whether it actually is.
Wrong: The scalar triple product test works with any direction vectors, including direction cosines (which are direction ratios of magnitude 1).
Correct: normalising \( \vec b_1 \) to direction cosines (T1 skill) doesn't change the direction, so the scalar triple product test (T5 skill) gives \( 6\neq 0 \).
